problem: The purpose clause ('lest in the passage from one faith to another...') is turned into two free-standing statements, so the logical link (do not replace old beliefs, because the soul may be left bare) is lost.
replacement: Most religions are simply general, simple, and practical ways of teaching men the doctrine of the immortality of the soul. That is the greatest benefit a democratic people gets from its belief, and so belief is more necessary to such a people than to any other. Therefore, when a religion has sunk its roots deep into a democracy, take care not to disturb them. Watch over it instead, as the most precious legacy of aristocratic ages. Do not try to replace men’s old religious opinions with new ones, for in passing from one faith to another the soul may be left for a while stripped of all belief, and the love of physical gratifications could then grow in it and fill it entirely.

problem: 'so many rich Americans' softened to 'Many'; 'some scattered remains' changed to 'a few scattered remains'.
replacement: Among a democratic people, where there is no hereditary wealth, every man works to earn a living, or has worked, or was born to parents who worked. The idea of labor is therefore presented to the mind on every side as the necessary, natural, and honest condition of human existence. Among such a people labor is not only not dishonorable; it is held in honor. The prejudice is not against it but in its favor. In the United States, a wealthy man thinks he owes it to public opinion to devote his leisure to some industrial or commercial pursuit, or to public business. He would think himself in bad repute if he spent his life merely living. So many rich Americans come to Europe to escape this obligation to work. There they find some scattered remains of aristocratic society, among which idleness is still held in honor.

problem: 'the State is shaken' rendered 'the nation itself' (term drift from state; the political body is meant); 'very unexpected' rendered 'sudden'.
replacement: The Americans advance enormously in productive industry because every one of them throws himself into it at the same time. For that very reason they face unexpected and formidable troubles. Everyone is in commerce, so their commercial affairs depend on causes too varied and tangled for anyone to predict what trouble may come. Everyone is more or less in productive industry, so at the slightest jolt to business every private fortune is endangered at once, and the state itself is shaken. I believe that these recurring commercial panics are a disease native to the democratic nations of our age. It can be made less dangerous, but it cannot be cured, since it springs not from accidents but from the temperament of these nations.
